items.new: The long and narrow peninsula of Malacca, extending southeast from the territories of Burma, forms the most southerly point of all Asia. In a continuous line from that peninsula stretch the long islands of Sumatra, Java, Bali, and Timor. These, with many others, form a vast mole, or rampart, lengthwise connecting Asia with Australia and dividing the long unbroken Indian Ocean from the densely studded eastern archipelagoes. This rampart is pierced by several sally-ports for the convenience of ships and whales, the most prominent being the Straits of Sunda and Malacca. By the Straits of Sunda, chiefly, vessels bound to China from the west emerge into the China seas.

items.new: Those narrow Straits of Sunda divide Sumatra from Java. Standing midway in that vast rampart of islands, buttressed by that bold green promontory known to seamen as Java Head, they closely resemble the central gateway opening into some vast walled empire. And considering the inexhaustible wealth of spices, silks, jewels, gold, and ivory with which the thousand islands of that eastern sea are enriched, it seems a significant provision of nature that such treasures, by the very formation of the land, should at least bear the appearance — however ineffective — of being guarded from the all-grasping western world. The shores of the Straits of Sunda are unsupplied with those domineering fortresses which guard the entrances to the Mediterranean, the Baltic, and the Propontis. Unlike the Danes, these Orientals do not demand the obsequious homage of lowered topsails from the endless procession of ships running before the wind that for centuries past, by night and day, have passed between the islands of Sumatra and Java, freighted with the costliest cargoes of the east. But while they freely waive such ceremony, they by no means renounce their claim to more solid tribute.

items.new: But what now? In this globe-girdling quest, does Ahab touch no land? Does his crew drink air? Surely he will stop for water. No. For a long time now, the circus-running sun has raced within his fiery ring and needs no sustenance but what is in himself. So with Ahab. Mark this, too, about the whaler. While other ships are loaded down with foreign goods to be transferred to distant wharves, the world-wandering whale-ship carries no cargo but herself and her crew, their weapons and their wants. She has a whole lake's contents bottled in her ample hold. She is ballasted with useful things, not entirely with useless pig-lead and ballast iron. She carries years' worth of water in her. Clear old prime Nantucket water, which, when three years at sea, the Nantucketer in the Pacific prefers to drink over the brackish fluid rafted off only yesterday in casks from Peruvian or Indian streams. Hence it is that while other ships may have gone to China from New York and back again, touching at a score of ports, the whale-ship in all that time may not have sighted one grain of soil — her crew having seen no man but floating seamen like themselves. So that if you brought them the news that another flood had come, they would only answer: "Well, boys, here's the ark!"

items.new: Stripped to our shirts and drawers, we sprang to the oars. After several hours' pulling, we were almost ready to give up the chase when a general pausing commotion among the whales gave encouraging signs that they were now under the influence of that strange paralysis of indecision which, when fishermen see it in a whale, they say he is gallied. The compact martial columns in which they had been rapidly and steadily swimming now broke apart in one measureless rout. Like King Porus's elephants in the Indian battle with Alexander, they seemed going mad with panic. Expanding in vast irregular circles in all directions, swimming aimlessly this way and that, they plainly showed their distracted terror by their short, thick spoutings. This was still more strangely shown by those among them who, completely paralyzed as it were, helplessly floated like waterlogged dismasted ships on the sea. Had these leviathans been but a flock of simple sheep pursued over a pasture by three fierce wolves, they could not possibly have shown such excessive dismay. But this occasional timidity is characteristic of almost all herding creatures. Though banding together in tens of thousands, the lion-maned buffaloes of the West have fled before a solitary horseman. Witness, too, all human beings — how when herded together in the sheepfold of a theater pit, they will at the slightest alarm of fire rush helter-skelter for the exits, crowding, trampling, jamming, and mercilessly crushing each other to death. Best, therefore, withhold any amazement at the strangely gallied whales before us, for there is no folly of the beasts of the earth which is not infinitely outdone by the madness of men.

items.new: Though many of the whales, as has been said, were in violent motion, as a whole the herd neither advanced nor retreated but collectively remained in one place. As is customary in such cases, the boats separated at once, each making for some lone whale on the outskirts of the shoal. In about three minutes, Queequeg's harpoon was flung. The stricken whale darted blinding spray in our faces, then ran away with us like light, steering straight for the heart of the herd. Though such a move by a harpooned whale is by no means unprecedented and indeed is almost always expected to some degree, it presents one of the more dangerous episodes of the fishery. For as the swift monster drags you deeper and deeper into the frantic shoal, you bid farewell to cautious living and exist only in a delirious throb.

items.new: All whaleboats carry certain curious devices, originally invented by the Nantucket Indians, called druggs. Two thick squares of wood of equal size are stoutly clenched together so that they cross each other's grain at right angles. A line of considerable length is then attached to the middle of this block, and the other end of the line, being looped, can in a moment be fastened to a harpoon. It is chiefly among gallied whales that this drugg is used. For then, more whales are close around you than you can possibly chase at one time. But sperm whales are not encountered every day, so while you can, you must kill all you can. And if you cannot kill them all at once, you must wound them so that they can be killed afterward at your leisure. Hence it is that at times like these the drugg comes into play. Our boat was furnished with three of them. The first and second were successfully thrown, and we saw the whales staggering off, fettered by the enormous sideways resistance of the towing drugg. They were hobbled like criminals with ball and chain. But upon flinging the third, in the act of tossing the clumsy wooden block overboard, it caught under one of the boat's seats and in an instant tore it out and carried it away, dumping the oarsman into the boat's bottom as the seat slid from under him. On both sides the sea poured in at the damaged planks, but we stuffed two or three pairs of drawers and shirts in, and so stopped the leaks for the time being.

items.new: It would have been nearly impossible to throw these drugged harpoons had our whale's pace not greatly slowed as we advanced into the herd. Moreover, as we went still further from the circumference of commotion, the chaos seemed to be waning. So when at last the jerking harpoon pulled free and the towing whale vanished sideways, we glided with the tapering force of his parting momentum between two whales into the innermost heart of the shoal — as if from some mountain torrent we had slid into a serene valley lake. Here the storms in the roaring glens between the outermost whales were heard but not felt. In this central expanse, the sea presented that smooth satin-like surface called a sleek, produced by the subtle moisture thrown off by the whale in his quieter moods. Yes, we were now in that enchanted calm which they say lurks at the heart of every commotion. And still in the distracted distance we saw the tumults of the outer concentric circles — successive pods of whales, eight or ten in each, swiftly going round and round like multiplied teams of horses in a ring, so closely shoulder to shoulder that a titanic circus-rider might easily have arched over the middle ones and ridden round on their backs. Owing to the density of the whales reposing more immediately around the trapped center of the herd, no possible chance of escape was presently offered to us. We had to watch for a breach in the living wall that hemmed us in — the wall that had only admitted us in order to shut us up. Keeping to the center of the lake, we were occasionally visited by small, tame cows and calves: the women and children of this routed host.

At any rate — though such a measurement at such a time might be deceptive — spouts could be seen from our low boat that seemed to play up almost from the rim of the horizon. I mention this because, as if the cows and calves had been purposely locked up in this innermost fold, and as if the wide extent of the herd had prevented them from learning the precise cause of its stopping — or possibly, being so young, unsophisticated, and in every way innocent and inexperienced — however it may have been, these smaller whales, now and then visiting our becalmed boat from the margin of the lake, showed a wondrous fearlessness and confidence, or else a spellbound panic that was impossible not to marvel at. Like household dogs, they came snuffling right up to our gunwales and touching them, until it almost seemed that some enchantment had suddenly domesticated them. Queequeg patted their foreheads. Starbuck scratched their backs with his lance, though, fearful of the consequences, he refrained from darting it for the time.

items.new: But far beneath this wondrous world upon the surface, another and still stranger world met our eyes as we gazed over the side. For suspended in those watery vaults floated the forms of nursing mother whales, and those that by their enormous girth seemed shortly to become mothers. The lake, as I have hinted, was to a considerable depth exceedingly transparent. And as human infants while suckling will calmly and fixedly gaze away from the breast, as if leading two different lives at the same time — while yet drawing mortal nourishment, still spiritually feasting upon some unearthly memory — even so did the young of these whales seem to look up toward us, but not at us, as if we were but a bit of Gulfweed in their newborn sight. Floating on their sides, the mothers also seemed quietly eyeing us. One of these little infants, that from certain signs seemed hardly a day old, might have measured some fourteen feet in length and six feet around. He was a little frisky, though his body seemed scarcely recovered from the irksome position it had so recently occupied in the maternal reticule — the womb pictured as a lady's drawstring bag — where, tail to head and all ready for the final spring, the unborn whale lies bent like a Tartar's bow. The delicate side-fins and the palms of his flukes still freshly retained the plaited, crumpled appearance of a baby's ears newly arrived from foreign parts.

items.new: *The sperm whale, like all other species of Leviathan but unlike most other fish, breeds indiscriminately at all seasons. After a gestation that may probably be set at nine months, it produces but one at a time, though in some few known instances giving birth to an Esau and Jacob — twins — a contingency provided for in suckling by two teats, curiously situated one on each side of the anus, though the breasts themselves extend upward from that point. When by chance these precious parts in a nursing whale are cut by the hunter's lance, the mother's pouring milk and blood, rivaling each other, discolor the sea for rods around. The milk is very sweet and rich. It has been tasted by man, and it might go well with strawberries. When overflowing with mutual esteem, the whales salute more hominum — in the manner of human beings.

items.new: Riotous and disordered as the universal commotion now was, it soon resolved itself into what seemed a systematic movement. Having clumped together at last in one dense body, the whales renewed their forward flight with increased speed. Further pursuit was useless, but the boats still lingered in their wake to pick up whatever drugged whales might be dropped behind, and also to secure one that Flask had killed and waifed. The waif is a pennoned pole — a pole carrying a small flag —, two or three of which are carried by every boat. When additional prey is at hand, these are inserted upright into the floating body of a dead whale, both to mark its place on the sea and as a token of prior possession, should the boats of any other ship draw near.

items.new: It frequently happens that when several ships are cruising together, a whale may be struck by one vessel, then escape, and finally be killed and captured by another. And within this general situation are many minor variations, all sharing this one feature. For example: after a weary and perilous chase and capture of a whale, the body may break loose from the ship in a violent storm and drift far to leeward, only to be retaken by a second whaler who, in a calm, snugly tows it alongside without risk of life or line. Thus the most maddening and violent disputes would often arise between fishermen, were there not some written or unwritten, universal, undisputed law applicable to all cases.

items.new: First: What is a Fast-Fish? Alive or dead, a fish is technically fast when it is connected with an occupied ship or boat by any medium at all controllable by the occupant or occupants — a mast, an oar, a nine-inch cable, a telegraph wire, or a strand of cobweb, it is all the same. Likewise, a fish is technically fast when it bears a waif or any other recognized symbol of possession, so long as the party waifing it plainly shows both its ability to take the fish alongside at any time, and its intention to do so.

items.new: Some fifty years ago there was a curious case of whale-trover litigated in England. The plaintiffs stated that after a hard chase of a whale in the northern seas, and when they had succeeded in harpooning the fish, they were at last, through peril of their lives, obliged to abandon not only their lines but their boat itself. Eventually the defendants — the crew of another ship — came up with the whale, struck, killed, seized, and finally claimed it before the very eyes of the plaintiffs. And when those defendants were confronted, their captain snapped his fingers in the plaintiffs' faces and assured them that by way of a doxology (a closing hymn of praise) to the deed he had done, he would now retain their line, harpoons, and boat, which had remained attached to the whale at the time of the seizure. Wherefore the plaintiffs sued for the recovery of the value of their whale, line, harpoons, and boat.

items.new: Mr. Erskine was counsel for the defendants; Lord Ellenborough was the judge. In the course of the defense, the witty Erskine went on to illustrate his position by alluding to a recent crim. con. case — a suit for adultery —, in which a gentleman, after in vain trying to bridle his wife's viciousness, had at last abandoned her upon the seas of life. But in the course of years, repenting of that step, he brought an action to recover possession of her. Erskine was on the other side and had then supported the case by saying that though the gentleman had originally harpooned the lady, and had once had her fast, and only by reason of the great stress of her plunging viciousness had at last abandoned her — yet abandon her he did, so that she became a Loose-Fish. And therefore when a subsequent gentleman re-harpooned her, the lady then became that subsequent gentleman's property, along with whatever harpoon might have been found sticking in her.

items.new: Is it not a saying on everyone's lips that possession is half the law — regardless of how the thing came into possession? But often possession is the whole of the law. What are the bodies and souls of Russian serfs and Republican slaves but Fast-Fish, of which possession is the whole of the law? What to the greedy landlord is the widow's last mite but a Fast-Fish? What is yonder undetected villain's marble mansion with a door-plate for a waif — what is that but a Fast-Fish? What is the ruinous discount that Mordecai the broker gets from poor Woebegone the bankrupt, on a loan to keep Woebegone's family from starving — what is that ruinous discount but a Fast-Fish? What is the Archbishop of Savesoul's income of a hundred thousand pounds, seized from the meager bread and cheese of hundreds of thousands of broken-backed laborers, all sure of heaven without any of Savesoul's help — what is that globular hundred thousand pounds but a Fast-Fish? What are the Duke of Dunder's hereditary towns and hamlets but Fast-Fish? What to that mighty harpooner John Bull is poor Ireland but a Fast-Fish? What to that apostolic lancer Brother Jonathan is Texas but a Fast-Fish? And concerning all these, is not Possession the whole of the law?

As we glided nearer, the stranger showed French colors from her peak. You can well imagine what an unsavory odor such a mass must give off — worse than an Assyrian city in the plague, when the living cannot bury the dead. So intolerable is it considered by some that no greed could persuade them to moor alongside it. Yet there are those who will still do it, notwithstanding the fact that the oil obtained from such subjects is of very inferior quality, and by no means of the nature of attar of roses.

items.new: I believe it is plainly traceable to the first arrival of the Greenland whaling ships in London, more than two centuries ago. Because those whalemen did not then, and do not now, render their oil at sea as the southern ships have always done. Instead, cutting up the fresh blubber in small bits, they thrust it through the bungholes of large casks and carry it home that way — the shortness of the season in those icy seas and the sudden, violent storms to which they are exposed forbidding any other course. The consequence is that upon breaking into the hold and unloading one of these whale cemeteries in the Greenland dock, a stench is released somewhat similar to that rising from excavating an old city graveyard for the foundations of a lying-in (maternity) hospital.

items.new: In outward appearance, Pip and Dough-Boy made a matched pair, like a black pony and a white one of equal size though different color, driven in one oddly matched team. But while hapless Dough-Boy was by nature dull and sluggish in his wits, Pip, though over tender-hearted, was at bottom very bright, with that pleasant, warm, jolly brightness peculiar to his tribe — a tribe who ever enjoy all holidays and festivities with finer, freer relish than any other race. For blacks, the year's calendar should show nothing but three hundred and sixty-five Fourth of Julys and New Year's Days. Nor smile while I write that this little black boy was brilliant, for even blackness has its brilliance: behold that lustrous ebony, paneled in kings' cabinets. But Pip loved life and all life's peaceful securities, so that the panic-striking business in which he had somehow become entangled had most sadly dimmed his brightness — though, as will soon be seen, what was thus temporarily subdued in him was destined in the end to be luridly illuminated by strange wild fires, that falsely showed him off to ten times the natural luster with which, in his native Tolland County in Connecticut, he had once enlivened many a fiddler's dance on the green and, at melodious twilight, with his gay ha-ha! had turned the round horizon into one star-belled tambourine. So, though in the clear light of day a pure diamond drop suspended against a blue-veined neck will glow with healthy beauty, yet when the cunning jeweler would show you the diamond in its most impressive luster, he lays it against a gloomy background and then lights it up not by the sun but by some unnatural gas. Then come those fiery blazes, infernally superb. Then the evil-blazing diamond, once the divinest symbol of the crystal skies, looks like some crown-jewel stolen from the King of Hell. But let us get to the story.
